articles.title: Adiós Leon XIV : la miniserie de 4 caps sobre los misterios de la fe que conquista Netflix
articles.summary: (BUENOS AIRES).- Netflix tiene disponible Misterios de la fe, una miniserie documental de cuatro episodios sobre algunas de las reliquias más sagradas del cristianismo. La producción recorre las histo
articles.content: (BUENOS AIRES).- Netflix tiene disponible Misterios de la fe, una miniserie documental de cuatro episodios sobre algunas de las reliquias más sagradas del cristianismo. La producción recorre las historias, creencias y controversias que rodean a esos objetos. Las piezas que aparecen en la serie estuvieron vinculadas con Jesús y con momentos importantes de la historia cristiana, según la tradición religiosa. El recorrido muestra cómo atravesaron los siglos y se convirtieron en símbolos de devoción para millones de creyentes. Para reconstruir esas historias, la miniserie combina investigaciones, testimonios y reconstrucciones. Uno de los episodios aborda la Corona de Espinas, que, según la tradición, fue colocada sobre la cabeza de Jesús durante la crucifixión. El documental también recuerda el incendio de la catedral de Notre Dame, en París, ocurrido en 2019. En ese contexto, repasa el operativo que permitió rescatar la reliquia de las llamas. El Santo Grial, la copa asociada con la Última Cena, aparece entre los grandes interrogantes de la producción. La serie explora distintas teorías sobre su posible paradero y presenta las versiones que rodean a esa reliquia. El objeto forma parte de un recorrido que combina la historia con las creencias vinculadas a los símbolos cristianos. La miniserie también se detiene en el Velo de Manoppello, una tela conservada en Italia. Algunos fieles le atribuyen una representación del rostro de Cristo. La producción incorpora esa creencia a su recorrido por objetos venerados y por las historias que se formaron alrededor de ellos. Otro tramo sigue la Vera Cruz, vinculada con la crucifixión de Jesús, y llega hasta Río de Janeiro, donde se conserva un fragmento de la reliquia. Las historias presentadas abren preguntas sobre la autenticidad de esos objetos y el lugar que ocupan dentro de la fe. La propuesta combina historia, investigación y espiritualidad para abordar esas cuestiones. La llegada del papa León XIV a Argentina el 8 de noviembre de 2026 volvió a poner a la Iglesia Católica y sus tradiciones en el centro de la atención. El pontífice tenía una agenda de encuentros y celebraciones hasta el miércoles 11. En ese marco, la miniserie aparece como una propuesta para quienes buscan profundizar en los símbolos y las historias del cristianismo, incluso fuera de las comunidades religiosas.

articles.content: El “Tomus ad Flavianum”: piedra angular del dogma cristológico León Magno fue un teólogo de precisión y profundidad extraordinarias. Su famosa carta doctrinal al patriarca Flaviano de Constantinopla —conocida como el Tomus ad Flavianum— definió con claridad la doctrina católica sobre las dos naturalezas de Cristo: divina y humana, unidas en una sola Persona. Este documento fue leído en el Concilio de Calcedonia (451) ante cientos de obispos que, al escucharlo, exclamaron: “Pedro ha hablado por boca de León.” Con esa expresión, la Iglesia universal reconocía el primado de la sede romana y la continuidad entre el Apóstol Pedro y sus sucesores. En tiempos en que el poder imperial pretendía someter la doctrina al control político, León reivindicó que la autoridad del Papa no depende del César ni de los concilios, sino de Cristo mismo, que prometió: “Tú eres Pedro, y sobre esta piedra edificaré mi Iglesia.” Gracias a su intervención, el Concilio de Calcedonia se convirtió en un hito de la ortodoxia cristológica y en un testimonio de la primacía del Romano Pontífice. El Papa León no impuso su autoridad con la fuerza, sino con la verdad; no por ambición humana, sino por fidelidad al depósito recibido. El Papa que detuvo a Atila En el año 452, la amenaza de los hunos llegó hasta las puertas de Italia. Atila, llamado “el azote de Dios”, había devastado Europa central y avanzaba hacia Roma. Sin ejército ni armas, León decidió ir al encuentro del invasor acompañado solo de algunos clérigos. El encuentro en el río Mincio, cerca de Mantua, se convirtió en uno de los episodios más sobrecogedores de la historia. La tradición narra que Atila, al ver al Papa, quedó sobrecogido por una fuerza sobrenatural y decidió retirarse. Algunos cronistas antiguos dicen que el caudillo vio detrás de León a los santos Pedro y Pablo empuñando espadas. Fuera cual fuera la causa, el hecho histórico es indiscutible: el Papa, solo con su autoridad moral, salvó a Roma de una destrucción segura. Tres años después, en el 455, León volvió a intervenir ante el vándalo Genserico, quien, aunque saqueó la ciudad, accedió a no incendiarla ni matar a sus habitantes. En una era de barbarie y desesperanza, el Papa se convirtió en defensor de la dignidad humana y de la civilización cristiana naciente. Un pastor de almas y doctor de la fe Más allá de los hechos históricos, el legado espiritual de León Magno se encuentra en sus Sermones y Cartas, textos que combinan rigor teológico, belleza retórica y profundidad pastoral. Sus homilías sobre la Encarnación y la Pascua son verdaderas joyas del pensamiento cristiano. En ellas resuena una teología que no separa la doctrina de la vida, ni la fe de la caridad. Fue también un reformador eclesial: disciplinó al clero, combatió los abusos, promovió la vida monástica y fortaleció la autoridad episcopal. Instituyó la solemnidad de la Natividad del Señor en Roma y consolidó la liturgia romana, que más tarde se extendería a toda la cristiandad. En un tiempo en que el caos amenazaba con disolver las instituciones, León mostró que la verdadera reforma de la Iglesia comienza en la santidad de sus pastores. De su espiritualidad brota una enseñanza perenne: el cristiano no puede dejarse arrastrar por el miedo ni por la confusión del mundo. Como escribió en una de sus homilías más célebres: “Reconoce, cristiano, tu dignidad. Y, puesto que has sido hecho partícipe de la naturaleza divina, no vuelvas a la antigua vileza con una conducta indigna.” En esas palabras se resume toda su visión: la fe no es una idea, sino una transformación de la persona; una participación real en la vida de Cristo. El Doctor que iluminó siglos León Magno murió el 10 de noviembre del año 461. Fue sepultado en la Basílica de San Pedro y proclamado Doctor de la Iglesia en el siglo XVIII por el Papa Benedicto XIV. Su influencia doctrinal se extendió por siglos y moldeó el pensamiento cristiano sobre el sacerdocio, la autoridad papal y la teología de la Encarnación. Su magi

articles.summary: Em seu penúltimo compromisso público desta segunda-feira (9) na Argentina, o papa Leão XIV liderou um encontro com representantes de diversas comunidades cristãs e tradições religiosas no Palácio San
articles.summary_zh: 教宗方济各于本周一（9日）在阿根廷的倒数第二次公开活动中，在圣米格尔宫与来自不同基督教社群和宗教传统的代表举行了会晤。
articles.title_zh: 利奥十四世捍卫宗教间对话，视其为人类尊严的守护者——梵蒂冈
articles.content: Em seu penúltimo compromisso público desta segunda-feira (9) na Argentina, o papa Leão XIV liderou um encontro com representantes de diversas comunidades cristãs e tradições religiosas no Palácio San Martín, em Buenos Aires. Em seu pronunciamento no Palácio San Martín, o pontífice americano homenageou seu antecessor, o papa Francisco, e destacou que o evento se realizou "nos pilares do diálogo e da amizade", elementos descritos como "fundamentais" na trajetória do antigo chefe da Igreja Católica. "Nosso encontro, de fato, se assenta nos pilares do diálogo e da amizade, que foram fundamentais na vida do Papa Francisco e que agora desejamos fortalecer, construindo novas pontes e novos caminhos de colaboração na sociedade em que vivemos", afirmou. Robert Francis Prevost ressaltou que a identidade nacional argentina "evoluiu como um caldeirão de diversas etnias, culturas e religiões, formada por povos originários e imigrantes de várias partes do mundo, que trouxeram consigo seus sonhos e sua fé: a princípio, católicos, evangélicos e judeus, e posteriormente muitos outros". "Todos eles, em sua diversidade, aprenderam a trabalhar juntos, a formar famílias e comunidades e a construir cidades em admirável simbiose com as tradições locais. Uniram a nação e perseguiram projetos comuns sem que as religiões jamais fossem fonte de divisão, mas sim ponto de convergência e compromisso compartilhado com a sociedade", observou. O pontífice estruturou sua reflexão a partir de três pilares centrais que emergem da oração sincera: "as religiões como guardiãs da dignidade humana, como expressões de nossa liberdade e como espaços para cultivar a esperança". "As religiões nos lembram que não somos feitos apenas de matéria: nossa carne contém um excedente de vida e significado. Esse mesmo desejo, que se transforma em grito e súplica, atesta que não viemos do nada e não fomos feitos para a morte. Dessa forma, as religiões salvaguardam a dignidade humana. Portanto, cada vez que orarmos, devemos cuidar daqueles que vivem ao nosso redor, traduzindo nossas palavras em fraternidade renovada", analisou. Ao fazer um apelo pela preservação ambiental e moral, Leão XIV exortou os líderes a defender o planeta: "Não destruamos com nossas próprias mãos o 'jardim' que o Criador nos confiou". O papa enfatizou ainda que a fé atua na construção da sociedade ao "educar as consciências e nos libertar dos ídolos", funcionando como um elo vivo entre gerações. "A própria palavra religião é eloquente a esse respeito: refere-se a religare, isto é, conectar, unir as pessoas. Essa relação sustenta nossa jornada através da história. Ao louvarmos a Deus pelo dom da esperança, devemos compartilhá-la com aqueles que sofrem na pobreza, que perderam o sentido da vida e com aqueles que desejam se comprometer com a renovação do mundo segundo a justiça", declarou. Ao encerrar o evento, Leão XIV recitou a oração deixada por Francisco "que compromete todos a fazer o bem". Após acender uma vela entregue por uma criança, o pontífice e as autoridades presentes observaram um minuto de silêncio em favor da paz mundial. TODOS OS DIREITOS RESERVADOS © Copyright ANSA

articles.title: El papa León XIV ya está en Argentina y el campo tuvo protagonismo en su primer discurso
articles.summary: Tras pasar por Uruguay, el papa León XIV inició este domingo su histórica gira de cuatro días por Argentina, que constituye la primera llegada de un líder de la Iglesia Católica mundial a nuestro país
articles.summary_zh: 在访问乌拉圭之后，教宗利奥十四世于本周日开启了为期四天的历史性阿根廷之行，这是全球天主教会领袖首次踏上我国的土地。
articles.title_zh: 教宗方济各已抵达阿根廷，他在首场讲话中重点谈及乡村问题。
articles.content: Tras pasar por Uruguay, el papa León XIV inició este domingo su histórica gira de cuatro días por Argentina, que constituye la primera llegada de un líder de la Iglesia Católica mundial a nuestro país desde Juan Pablo II en 1987. En ese marco, la primera actividad del Sumo Pontífice fue un discurso en el Palacio Libertad de la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires (CABA), frente al presidente de la Nación, Javier Milei. Y aunque sus palabras lógicamente estuvieron apuntadas hacia toda la sociedad, hubo numerosos pasajes que encontraron especial sintonía con el mundo agropecuario. Esto, en la previa de la reunión que León XIV mantendrá el lunes con representantes empresariales, sindicales y de organizaciones sociales, entre los que estarán los presidentes de las cuatro entidades de la Mesa de Enlace. EL PAPA LEÓN XIV EN ARGENTINA Puntualmente, el jefe mayor del Vaticano destacó el valor del esfuerzo cotidiano de los argentinos, con una mención expresa a quienes trabajan en el campo, y reivindicó la importancia de generar oportunidades, estimular la iniciativa privada y aprovechar responsablemente los recursos naturales. “Esta tierra conoce bien el valor del esfuerzo de quienes se ganan la vida en el campo y en las ciudades”, expresó León XIV, al destacar también el papel de los emprendedores y de las familias que sostienen sus hogares a través del trabajo. Asimismo, el Papa reconoció el enorme potencial productivo del país, al señalar que la Argentina cuenta con una extraordinaria riqueza natural, desde sus campos y reservas de agua hasta sus fuentes de energía, minerales y biodiversidad. Así, su mensaje combinó la posibilidad de aprovechar esos recursos para generar desarrollo y bienestar con la responsabilidad de preservar el ambiente y las condiciones de vida de las futuras generaciones. También dedicó un espacio a la innovación, la investigación y las nuevas tecnologías, incluida la inteligencia artificial, destacando su capacidad para transformar la producción y mejorar la vida de las personas. Por otro lado, al expresar una mirada sobre América del Sur, mencionó además a los alimentos, la energía y el conocimiento como elementos que vinculan a los países y abren oportunidades para fortalecer la cooperación regional. LEON XIV, EL MARTÍN FIERO Y EL MATE Asimismo, León XIV ofreció referencias cargadas de simbolismo para la identidad argentina. Por ejemplo, mencionó al Martín Fierro de José Hernández, a Jorge Luis Borges, al tango y a las tradiciones del interior del país. Y no faltó una de las costumbres más arraigadas entre los argentinos: el mate compartido, al que presentó como un gesto cotidiano que favorece la conversación y la cercanía. Por último, hacia el final de su intervención, León XIV evocó a Nuestra Señora de Luján, patrona de la Argentina y figura de especial significado para las comunidades rurales y para generaciones de familias de todo el país. También recordó al papa Francisco, citó a Carlos Gardel y alentó a los argentinos a valorar el patrimonio recibido de las generaciones anteriores y trabajar para dejar un país mejor a quienes vendrán. De esta manera, sin ser un discurso específicamente dirigido al agro, las palabras de León XIV dejaron un reconocimiento al trabajo rural, a la producción, a la iniciativa emprendedora y a las tradiciones que forman parte de la identidad argentina. Un mensaje que también llegó al corazón del campo argentino. EL DISCURSO COMPLETO DEL PAPA LEÓN XIV Señor Presidente de la República, distinguidas autoridades y miembros del cuerpo diplomático. Señoras y señores, me alegra profundamente encontrarme hoy en esta querida tierra argentina. Agradezco, señor Presidente, las cordiales palabras que ha tenido a bien dirigirme y la acogida que por medio de usted me brinda su pueblo. Saludos también a los miembros del cuerpo diplomático y a las demás autoridades aquí presentes, y extiendo con afecto mi saludo a todos los argentinos. articles.title_zh: 《国家报》/圣洛伦索教区迎来新主教
articles.content: El papa León XIV nombró a monseñor Pierre Jubinville como nuevo obispo de la diócesis de San Lorenzo en reemplazo de monseñor Joaquín Robledo, quien presentó renuncia al cargo. La Nunciatura Apostólica en Paraguay comunicó el sábado 7 de noviembre que el santo padre aceptó la renuncia de Robledo y designó en su reemplazo a monseñor Pierre Laurent Jubinville, quien se desempeñaba como obispo de San Pedro y es el actual presidente de la Conferencia Episcopal Paraguaya (CEP). La decisión fue anunciada por la CEP, conforme a lo establecido en el Código de Derecho Canónico, que contempla la renuncia de los obispos al alcanzar los 75 años de edad. No obstante, monseñor Robledo continuará al frente de la diócesis como administrador apostólico hasta la toma de posesión canónica de su sucesor. La Conferencia Episcopal Paraguaya agradeció a monseñor Robledo por su servicio pastoral y dedicación a la Iglesia, al tiempo que encomendó en oración al nuevo obispo, deseándole un fecundo ministerio episcopal en su nueva misión. El nuevo obispo Monseñor Pierre Laurent Jubinville nació el 5 de agosto de 1960 en Ottawa, Canadá. Tras algunas experiencias laborales, ingresó en la Congregación del Espíritu Santo y estudió Teología en la Universidad de Montreal. Emitió los votos solemnes en 1988 y fue ordenado presbítero el 17 de setiembre de 1988. Tras algunas experiencias misioneras en África, realizó estudios académicos en Montreal y París. Llegó a Paraguay en 1991, desarrolló diversas tareas pastorales y formativas; entre ellas, se desempeñó en la pastoral indígena de la parroquia San José Obrero, en la Diócesis de San Pedro; fue párroco de San Francisco de Asís y formador de la Congregación del Espíritu Santo en Asunción. En 2013 fue nombrado obispo de San Pedro y recibió la ordenación episcopal el 21 de diciembre de ese mismo año. Además, ejerció la vicepresidencia de la Conferencia Episcopal Paraguaya entre 2018 y 2024 y, desde noviembre de 2024, ocupa la presidencia de dicha institución. La Diócesis de San Lorenzo comprende varias localidades del departamento Central, entre ellas Capiatá, San Lorenzo, Ñemby, Itá, Ypané, Guarambaré, Villeta, Nueva Italia, San Antonio, J. Augusto Saldívar, Ypacaraí y Thompson.

articles.title: Why Did Prosecutors Agree To Omit References to Katy Perry From the Opening Statements at Trial ?
articles.summary: Prosecutors agreed to remove references to Katy Perry from their opening statement at Russell Brand's London rape trial after objections from his lawyers. The decision emerged on Thursday, 5 November
articles.summary_zh: 在拉塞尔·布兰德的伦敦强奸案庭审中，经其律师提出异议，检方同意从开庭陈述中删除提及凯蒂·佩里的内容。该决定于11月5日星期四公布。
articles.title_zh: 为什么检察官同意在庭审开场陈述中省略对凯蒂·佩里的提及？
articles.content: Prosecutors agreed to remove references to Katy Perry from their opening statement at Russell Brand's London rape trial after objections from his lawyers. The decision emerged on Thursday, 5 November 2026, after a jury returned verdicts at Southwark Crown Court. Brand, 51, was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women. Jurors acquitted him of two further rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. He had denied all seven charges, which concerned six women. Details of the pretrial discussions became public after reporting restrictions ended. They showed how Brand's former marriage was kept out of the prosecution's opening address, although he later mentioned Perry while giving evidence. Why Katy Perry References Were Removed From the Opening Lead prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC acknowledged in written submissions that references to Brand's relationship with Perry after 2009 'may be sensitive'. According to Sky News' court reporting, prosecutors were 'content to remove these from the opening' following defence submissions. The agreement was limited to the opening statement. It did not prevent every mention of Perry during the proceedings or establish that the relationship itself was evidence of wrongdoing. Perry was not accused of any offence. Prosecutors also agreed to leave out references to Brand's earlier religious beliefs and his 2024 baptism. His Christian conversion was nevertheless mentioned during questioning of his wife, Laura, showing that the restrictions on the opening did not cover all subsequent testimony. Other arguments before the trial concerned references to Brand's past drug and alcohol use. His lawyers challenged their relevance to the allegations, and material about treatment at a sex addiction clinic was omitted from a former assistant's evidence. Those disputes were separate from the agreement concerning Perry. The Crown Prosecution Service confirmed that investigators had not asked Perry for a witness statement. Senior Crown Prosecutor David Roberts said reasonable lines of inquiry relevant to the charges had been pursued. There is no basis in that statement to suggest Perry refused to cooperate. Katy Perry's Marriage Still Entered the Courtroom Perry and Brand began dating in 2009 and married in Rajasthan, India, in 2010. They separated in December 2011, and their divorce was finalised in 2012. The offences for which Brand was convicted took place between 2004 and 2009. During his evidence, Brand referred to the marriage and said it had brought him 'staggering fame'. The comment arose from his own testimony, not the prosecution's opening statement. It did not turn Perry into a witness or complainant. The Crown Prosecution Service said the women whose cases resulted in convictions came forward independently after a television investigation aired in September 2023. Prosecutors relied on their accounts and testimony from other witnesses to present evidence of Brand's conduct. Following the verdict, Roberts said Brand had 'used his celebrity status to commit sexual crimes'. The agency thanked the women for coming forward and stressed that sexual offences can be prosecuted years after they occur. The complainants have lifelong anonymity. Mr Justice Joel Bennathan refused Brand bail and remanded him in custody ahead of sentencing on Monday, 9 November. The judge warned that he faced a 'significant custodial term'. Rape carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment in England and Wales. © Copyright IBTimes 2026. All rights reserved.

articles.content: Antes de escribir la biografía de Jorge Bergoglio, que llamó El gran Reformador, Austen Ivereigh ya era un experto en la historia de la Iglesia argentina. “Mi tesis de doctorado [en Oxford], que terminé en el 92, fue sobre catolicismo y política en la Argentina”. Y hay más: “Debo mi fe a la Iglesia Argentina, leyendo artículos de monseñor (Gustavo) Franceschi, volví a la fe”, dice. Ese conocimiento de nuestro país y de su fe mayoritaria representó una ventaja a la hora de escribir sobre Bergoglio, ya que cada etapa de la trayectoria del futuro Papa está debidamente contextualizada en la época que atravesaba el país. Desde aquel marzo de 2013, cuando la novedad de un pontífice argentino y jesuita impactó al mundo entero, Ivereihg siempre pensó que vendría cuando Francisco visitara la Argentina, viaje que finalmente no se concretó. “Ahora vengo con León”, comenta. En efecto, este escritor, historiador, periodista y analista de asuntos religiosos y políticos estará en nuestro país contemporáneamente con la visita del papa León XIV, invitado por la Universidad del Salvador (USAL), donde dictó, el pasado viernes 6, una clase magistral sobre “El giro latinoamericano Francisco-León: la Iglesia misionera sinodal y el cambio de época”. Ivereigh también es co-autor de Let Us Dream (Soñemos Juntos, 2020), un libro escrito en colaboración con Francisco. Su trabajo más reciente es First Belong to God: On Retreat with Pope Francis (Lo primero es pertenecer a Dios: Un retiro con el Papa Francisco, 2024), basado en los escritos y charlas de Bergoglio como director espiritual de un retiro ignaciano de 8 días. De 2004 a 2006, Ivereigh fue colaborador del entonces arzobispo de Westminster, cardenal Cormac Murphy-O’Connor, uno de los más activos promotores de la candidatura de Jorge Mario Bergoglio al papado. Ivereigh considera que el papado de Francisco inició un giro latinoamericano hacia una iglesia misionera y sinodal, cuyo primer paso fue la exhortación apostólica Evangelii Gaudium (noviembre de 2013), sobre “el anuncio del Evangelio en el mundo actual”, con la cual, dice, “Francisco inaugura una hoja de ruta de su Papado que también es la del pontificado de León”. Pero esa hoja de ruta tenía una génesis anterior: el ya famoso documento de Aparecida, la V Conferencia General del Episcopado Latinoamericano y del Caribe (Celam), redactado por Bergoglio. De esta manera, “América Latina pasó a ser la iglesia fuente”, señala, porque “siempre hay una parte de la Iglesia de la cual brota un dinamismo teológico”. Antes, ese rol lo cumplía Europa, pero a partir del Concilio Vaticano II eso cambia porque es en América Latina donde mejor se lo pone en práctica. Aclara que “fuente” no quiere decir centro; de hecho, “Francisco quería una Iglesia multipolar”. — ¿Hasta qué punto Aparecida refleja a Bergoglio como individualidad y hasta dónde es la Iglesia latinoamericana, que usted define como “fuente”? — El proceso de preparación de esa conferencia general, fue muy sinodal, de mucha consulta, y el papel de Bergoglio en esa conferencia general es muy conocido. Creo que influyó la recepción del Concilio Vaticano II en el Río de La Plata, que tuvo un matiz distinto al resto de América Latina. Tal vez, cuando llegó a Aparecida esa visión sobre la religiosidad popular estaba ya madura. Es decir, una teología de espiritualidad latinoamericana, distinta a anteriores teologías latinoamericanas. Bergoglio tenía muchas cosas que eran de él. Pero también llevaba en su forma de ser y de pensar muchos aportes de la iglesia argentina, la influencia de Lucio Gera y de Rafael Tello y toda esa tradición. — ¿Cómo vio el impacto de su papado en la Argentina? — Creo que una de las razones por las que no vino, sobre todo al principio, fue que tenía horror del triunfalismo. Y sabía que tal vez los argentinos tenían —todos los países lo tienen— una cierta tentación de decir: “El Papa es argentino”. articles.summary_zh: 2026年11月7日，教宗利奥十四世抵达蒙得维的亚百年体育场参加祈祷守夜活动，他在教宗座驾上向信众挥手致意。（法新社照片）教宗利奥十四世于11月7日告诫学生们
articles.title_zh: 教皇警告人工智能会导致非人性化
articles.content: Pope Leo XIV waves to faithful from the popemobile upon his arrival for a prayer vigil at the Centenario Stadium in Montevideo on November 7, 2026. (AFP Photo) Pope Leo XIV warned students on Nov. 7 of “dehumanization” through the use of AI in education, and urged schools and university to place the “person before the algorithm.” “The process of dehumanization we are experiencing poses a challenge,” the pope, who has warned repeatedly about the need to ensure AI is used ethically, said in a speech at the Catholic University of Uruguay. Just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the 71-year-old pontiff is on a 12-day tour of South Africa where he served nearly two decades as a missionary. On Nov. 7, he visited the crime-blighted Montevideo neighborhood of Casavalle. The murder rate in the impoverished district is four times the national average and residents spoke movingly of the dangers they faced, like commonplace gun violence. Katherine Silva’s voice cracked with emotion as she told the pope about the violence and abuse she had suffered as a child. After ending up homeless at 15, the young mother said she “went through very dark times” and “nearly died.” “There are children in Uruguay who do not go to school for fear of never returning home,” Leo said. “In a country as rich in resources as this, children should never have to go to bed hungry... Much less should they have to suffer violence to the point of losing their lives,” he added. As police helicopters flew overhead, locals waved and cheered to welcome the head of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, who blessed 12 new low-income houses financed by the Church.

articles.title_zh: 世界各地的地标建筑将在2026年红色周期间亮灯
articles.content: About 130 cathedrals, thousands of churches, and over 125,000 people around the world are expected to take part in Red Week this month, with the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, honoring the occasion by lighting up in red on Nov. 23. Red Week 2026 will take place from Nov. 15–22, with Red Wednesday falling on Nov. 18 in most regions, although it will be observed on Nov. 25 in the Philippines. The observance began in 2016 by Aid to the Church in Need (ACN), an international Catholic aid organization and Pontifical Foundation of the Church that supports Christians who are persecuted, oppressed, or in material need. The week includes illuminating monuments in red, prayer vigils, testimonies, and seminars on Christian persecution around the world. Designed to raise awareness of the ongoing Christian persecution in countries particularly in Africa and Asia, Red Week brings together those who are persecuted and those who are working to end violence and hatred against people of faith. At various events, testimonials from survivors of religious persecution will provide powerful moments of reflection about the suffering and human rights violations happening around us that go unnoticed. According to the latest figures provided by ACN, 413 million Christians live in countries where serious violations of religious freedom occur, and around 220 million Christians worldwide are directly exposed to persecution. "Faced with this reality, the pontifical foundation is once again promoting the Red Week this November, an international mobilization of prayer, witness, and awareness-raising to draw attention to the deterioration of religious freedom and remember the millions of Christians who suffer discrimination and persecution because of their faith," said Regina Lynch, executive president of ACN International. Red is more than a color According to ACN's "Religious Freedom in the World Report 2025," more than 5.4 billion people — almost two-thirds of humanity — live in countries where religious freedom is not fully guaranteed. The color red is used to symbolize the blood of martyrs and all those who suffer for their faith. In 33 countries Christians have been forced to leave their homes because of their faith while in 57 countries Christians suffer physical violence or even detention because of their faith. Each church and monument taking part in Red Week serves as a reminder of Christians who cannot freely practice their religion. In line with article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, every individual has the freedom of thought, religion, and conscience with the right to practice their beliefs, free from persecution and violence. Through this weeklong initiative, ACN aims to promote one shared goal of making visible the shared suffering of the Christian people and defend everyone's fundamental rights to religious freedom.

articles.title: Revd Beilieü Shüya : The Pioneer of Christian Revival Church in Arunachal Pradesh
articles.summary: Revd Beilieü Shüya (15.8.1928 to 18.9.2026), remembered as the first CRC woman to be ordained, passed away at the age of 98 in Kohima, leaving behind a remarkable legacy of Christian faith, missionary
articles.content: Revd Beilieü Shüya (15.8.1928 to 18.9.2026), remembered as the first CRC woman to be ordained, passed away at the age of 98 in Kohima, leaving behind a remarkable legacy of Christian faith, missionary commitment, education, and service. Her life was a testimony to perseverance, spiritual conviction, and obedience to the call of GOD, extending her influence beyond Nagaland into Arunachal Pradesh. The eldest of ten children of Lhousuohie Shüya and Zeno Dolie Shüya of Meriema village, she belonged to a family closely connected with the region’s Christian history. Her maternal grandfather was reportedly the second person from Khonoma village to embrace Christianity. Her mother was also the sister of Angami Zapu Phizo, the legendary Naga nationalist leader. An Exceptional Educational Journey Revd Shüya received her early education at Mission School, Kohima, before continuing her studies at Mission School, Golaghat, Government High School, Kohima, and Cotton College, Guwahati. She completed the first two years of her Bachelor of Arts degree at Scottish Church College, Calcutta, and her final year at Tribhuvan University, Nepal. Her academic achievements extended across several disciplines. She obtained a diploma from the International Montessori Association, Kolkata, completed a Perspective Course in Education at William Carey University, California, earned a Bachelor of Education degree from Utkal University, Bhubaneswar, and pursued a Master of Theology at Los Angeles University. She also earned a Master of Arts in Tenyidie from Ura Academy. Her educational background reflected a lifelong commitment to learning, teaching, and the development of people through knowledge and faith. A Life Transformed By The Holy Spirit A defining moment in her spiritual journey came in 1946, when she experienced what she described as the filling of the Holy Spirit. From then on, her life became increasingly devoted to Christian ministry rather than earthly popularity or recognition. In 1978, she was ordained at the World Mission Conference in Chennai, becoming the first CRC woman to receive ordination, according to accounts of her life. Her ordination represented a significant milestone for CRC women in Christian ministry and demonstrated her determination to serve despite the social and institutional challenges of her time. Her Christian convictions also brought hardship. She was imprisoned for her faith and reportedly imprisoned again in 1956 because of her family connection with A. Z. Phizo. During periods of imprisonment in Kohima, Nagaon, and Guwahati, she translated numerous passages of the Bible. Even confinement could not silence her commitment to GOD’S Word. Bringing The Revival Movement To Arunachal Pradesh Among her most significant contributions was her involvement in introducing the Christian revival movement to Arunachal Pradesh. Along with a few fellow believers and missionary friends, she helped bring a new spiritual impetus to Christian communities in the state. According to personal recollections, the early team undertook three days of fasting in a forest, seeking GOD’S guidance and spiritual empowerment. This pioneering work contributed to the establishment of the Christian Revival Church in Arunachal Pradesh. Her missionary journeys were not without opposition. There were occasions when the police reportedly attempted to arrest her for preaching the gospel in the state. Nevertheless, she continued her mission, demonstrating courage and perseverance in the face of persecution. I still vividly remember the excitement surrounding the visits of Miss Beilieü Shüya and Miss Rose, a missionary from Goa, to Jipu. People would say that GOD was going to perform signs, wonders, and miracles through their ministry. In Siji, where the community had embraced Christianity, the atmosphere within our families and the wider village was filled with spiritual enthusiasm and expectation. featured.title_zh: 数字化之门为东南亚岛民打开福音之门
featured.content: Just as young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than in person, the same is true for people in Southeast Asia. IMB missionaries are creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content to connect with the lost through the internet. IMB Photo Recently, an International Mission Board team in Southeast Asia asked a young woman if she had heard the story of Jesus. She replied that, yes, she had heard about Him through a video online! “Back in the day,” shared Amanda Clarkston, an IMB missionary who has served in Southeast Asia for 33 years, “when I first came on the field, you’d go somewhere and gather all the people together in the village to watch the JESUS film.” Now, face-to-face conversations about Christ on the Southeast Asian islands are harder to accomplish. While teams travel to these remote islands often, living in a sparsely populated, animistic background culture as a foreigner creates suspicion and make long-term ministry difficult. Furthermore, young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than they are in person, Clarkston said, which is true of the islanders as well. Attempting to have a spiritual conversation face-to-face has become “too much” for locals, Clarkston shared. So, how do you share the gospel with multiple people groups who are constantly online and less comfortable with in-person interactions? For these Southeast Asia teams, digital engagement — the use of social media platforms to share a message — has become a plausible and effective entry point. The social media agency We Are Social confirmed this, revealing that 82.4% of Southeast Asia’s population uses the internet. “No matter where they go, how far they go, how remote it is, people have phones,” Clarkston and her team realized, “And though sometimes they do have to climb up the highest peak to get reception, people do it.” Clarkston’s team has begun creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content in hopes of building bridges to the islanders through the internet. Viewers can click on the ad to message back and forth with a responder, a local believer or missionary who is available to pray, build relationships and answer spiritual questions. “It seems like locals are more open to watching those things in the privacy of their own cell phones,” Clarkston said. Clarkston intends to use digital engagement as a means for initial contact with people with animistic backgrounds, evangelism and, eventually, discipleship. She said that this new ministry has the potential to open doors with individuals across these islands who would normally never reach out on their own or respond to the gospel in person. “Maybe they’ll respond this way,” Clarkston said, “I know without a shadow of a doubt that God is calling people to Himself.” Now, more than ever, technology has a grip on society. Many spend hours each day mindlessly scrolling, searching for meaning, for happiness. And now, more than ever, there is an incredible opportunity to plant seeds across Southeast Asian islands through digital engagement. The IMB Southeast Asia team gives praise to the Lord that He has provided a creative way to reach the lost and plant seeds. Pray the people among the Southeast Asian islands would see these ads and engage with responders boldly, even though they may face persecution or harm because of it. Names were changed for security. Mikah Young is serving overseas with the IMB. The work of the IMB is sustained through faithful giving to the Cooperative Program and the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering ® . featured.content_zh: 正如今天的年轻人对在线交谈比亲自交谈更加自在,东南亚人民也是如此。 IMB传教士正在创作并出版以耶稣为主的广告,视频等数字内容,以通过互联网与失落者相接. 最近,东南亚国际使团委员会的一个小组问一名年轻妇女是否听说过耶稣的故事。 她回答说,是的,她通过网络视频听到了他的消息! “回到今天 ” , 分享了IMB在东南亚服役了33年的传教士阿曼达·克拉克斯顿(Amanda Clarkston ) , “ 当我第一次来到现场时,你会去一个地方,把村里的所有人聚集在一起观看JESUS电影。 ” 现在,关于东南亚岛屿上的基督的面对面对话更难完成。 虽然各小组经常前往这些偏远岛屿,但作为外国人生活在人口稀少的厌世主义背景文化中,这造成了怀疑,使长期部委变得困难。 此外,克拉克斯顿说,今天的年轻人对在线交谈比他们本人感到更加自在,岛上居民也是如此。 Clarkston分享, 试图面对面进行精神对话, 所以,你如何与多个人群体分享福音呢? 他们经常在线,对亲身互动不太满意。 对于这些东南亚小组来说,数字参与——利用社交媒体平台分享信息——已成为一个可信而有效的切入点。 东南亚82.4%的人口使用互联网。 克拉克斯顿和她的团队意识到,“尽管有时他们必须爬上最高的山峰才能得到接待,但人们还是这么做了。” Clarkston的团队开始创作和发布以耶稣为焦点的广告,视频等数字内容,希望通过互联网为岛民搭起桥梁. 取景者可以点击广告,与回复者,当地信众或传教士相接来回留言,他们可以进行祈祷,建立关系并回答精神问题. Clarkston说, “当地人似乎更愿意在手机的隐私中观看这些东西。 克拉克斯顿打算用数字化的接战作为与有动画背景,福音派,并最终有门徒身份的人进行初步接触的手段. 她说,这个新的部有可能对这些岛屿上的个人敞开大门,他们通常不会独自伸出援手或亲自回应福音。 “也许他们会以这种方式回应,”克拉克斯顿说,“我毫不怀疑地知道,上帝正在号召人们投靠自己。 ” 现在,技术比以往更加控制社会。 许多人每天花上数小时无所顾忌地滚动,寻找意义,追求幸福. 现在,比以往任何时候,通过数字化参与,在东南亚各岛屿播种种子的机会比以往任何时候都多。 IMB东南亚队称赞了"主",他为到达失落地并播下种子提供了创造性的方法. 请东南亚各岛屿人民看到这些广告,并大胆地与回应者接触,尽管他们可能因此而面临迫害或伤害。 更改了安全名称。 米卡·杨在IMB海外服役. featured.title: How We Saw God’s Goodness Through Our Child’s Cancer
featured.summary: It was not in the good moments where God’s care was most evident. It was in the dark moments, often at night, when we were unsure if our son would survive.
featured.summary_zh: 这不是在神的关怀最明显的美好时刻。在黑暗的时刻，通常是在晚上，我们不确定我们的儿子是否能活下来。
featured.title_zh: 我们如何从孩子的癌症中看到神的良善
featured.content: To encounter profound suffering is to wrestle with isolation. From Job’s seat in the ashes to your neighbor’s loss, news of suffering often includes a struggle to connect. Our family’s cancer journey was like that. We felt alone. And we sensed disconnection—even helplessness—from people who heard the news. Childhood cancer is a blessedly uncommon experience, but navigating pain is inherent to life in a fallen world. When we encounter others’ pain, we have a “Good Samaritan choice”—to step forward and show compassion or to walk away. Nightmare Our 3-year-old son, Ben, had an unexplained illness. After a week in the hospital, we were ushered into an ICU conference room full of doctors and nurses. They delivered the news: “Your son has cancer.” One of the nurses was crying before they even said a word. Our family is from Washington, DC, but we were about 10,000 miles from home. We’d been serving as missionaries in Costa Rica, yet we weren’t there either. On that January day, we were in a hospital in Sydney, Australia, on our dream trip—a family Christmas in summertime. It was quickly becoming a nightmare. The days after the diagnosis were filled with rapid changes. We couldn’t go back to Costa Rica. Returning to DC was almost impossible. The Ronald McDonald House was our new home. My daughter started kindergarten at a new school, in a new country. She drew a picture of her family. There was no home, garden, or pets—just a hospital bed. Ben on his last day of chemotherapy / Courtesy of Peter Morris Over the next six months, Ben endured 96 nights in the hospital, 25 general anesthetics, and chemotherapy so strong it could blind or even kill an adult. He was traveling through the metaphorical valley of the shadow of death, and it was decorated with bright colors and superhero stickers. May 22 is a day we still celebrate in our family as “no more chemo day.” Ben took his final dose of chemotherapy, and we rejoiced with a trip to McDonald’s and a chocolate cake. Despite the celebration, the years ahead held mortal peril. His doctor told us relapse was a risk without a treatment plan. All we could do was watch and wait. Ben was immunocompromised for the years that followed, extending into the 2020s when the disruption of a health crisis—previously rare—became globally mundane. Today, Ben’s body still carries the scars of his cancer and the side effects of the lifesaving treatment he received. But he’s a survivor. To any passerby, he looks like an ordinary 12-year-old boy. My wife and I have scars too. But we also carry the lessons the Lord taught us along the way. Those lessons are available to all believers as we encounter the pain of others. Here are three that stand out. 1. You can’t depend on people. Suffering has an odd way of resetting relationships. We saw it repeatedly, in our experience and with other cancer families we met. The apparent uniqueness of the suffering—and the emotional reactions it stirred—drove some people away. They wouldn’t, or couldn’t, step close and walk with us. However, those people stepping away opened the door to gospel opportunities for us. Australian hospitals rarely have private rooms, so we spent most of our 96 nights sharing rooms with people from diverse cultures and faiths. As other people pulled back from them, we were able to step forward and hold out the hope of the gospel in a dark and hopeless place. 2. You can depend on people. While some in our life pulled away, others chose to pull close. We were thousands of miles from our church family, but people still found ways to care for us. When we shared the news about Ben’s illness, our Facebook post reached more than 15,000 people around the world. It wasn’t the eyeballs that made a difference but the thoughtful actions. Local believers jumped into action with a meal roster. Costa Rican friends translated our English updates to equip our Spanish-speaking friends to pray. American friends prepared care packages, sent encouraging texts, and came
featured.content_zh:
面对深刻的痛苦就是与孤立相搏。 从乔布在灰烬中的座位到邻居的损失, 我们家族的癌症旅程就是这样。 我们感到孤独。 我们感到与那些听到消息的人断绝关系,甚至是无助的。

童年时期的癌症是一种吉祥的罕见经历,但航海痛苦是堕落世界中生命所固有的. 当我们遇到其他人的痛苦时,我们有一个“好撒玛利亚人的选择”——站出来表示同情或离开。 噩梦我们3岁的儿子,本,有一个无法解释的疾病。 在医院里呆了一个星期后,我们被带入了一个由医生和护士组成的ICU会议室.

他们播下了一个消息:“你的儿子得了癌症。 其中一个护士甚至还没说一句话就哭了. 我们的家庭来自华盛顿特区 但我们离家约一万英里 我们一直担任哥斯达黎加的传教士, 1月当天,我们在澳大利亚悉尼的一家医院进行梦想之旅——夏天是家庭圣诞节。

它很快变成了一场噩梦。 诊断后的几天充满了快速的变化. 我们无法回到哥斯达黎加。 返回华盛顿几乎是不可能的。 罗纳德麦当劳之家是我们的新家 我女儿在新学校开始上幼儿园, 在新国家。 她画了一张她家人的照片。 没有家,没有花园,也没有宠物,只有一张医院床。

本最后一天的化疗 / 彼得・莫里斯的礼仪 在接下来的六个月里,本在医院忍受了96个晚上,25个一般麻醉药,化疗如此强大,可以盲目甚至杀死成人. 他穿梭在死亡阴影的隐喻山谷中,装饰着明亮的颜色和超级英雄贴纸.

5月22日仍是我们家庭庆祝的一天, Ben接受了最后的化疗, 尽管有庆典, 未来的岁月仍然有致命的危险。 他的医生告诉我们 复发是一种风险 没有治疗计划。 我们能做的就是观察和等待。

其后的几年里,本被免疫妥协,一直延续到2020年代,以前罕见的一次健康危机的破坏成为全球风云。 今天,Ben的身体仍带有癌症的伤疤和他接受救生治疗的副作用。 但他是个幸存者。 对于任何路人来说,他看起来像一个普通的12岁男孩. 我妻子和我也有伤疤

但我们也带着上帝教给我们的教训 当我们遇到其他人的痛苦时,所有信徒都可以接受这些教训。 这是三个突出的。 1. 你不能依赖人。 受苦有怪异的重构关系方式. 我们从我们的经验和我们遇到的其他癌症家庭中反复看到。

痛苦的明显独特性——以及它激起的情绪反应——驱赶一些人。 他们不会或无法靠近我们, 然而,那些走开的人为我们带来了机会。 澳大利亚的医院很少有私人房间,因此我们在96个晚上的大部分时间都与来自不同文化和信仰的人共用房间.

当其他人从他们那里撤退时,我们得以挺身而出,在一个黑暗和无望的地方抓住福音的希望。 2. 你可以依赖人。 在我们生命中有些人被拉走时,另一些人选择拉近。 我们离教会家数千英里 但人们仍然想方设法照顾我们

当我们分享本病的消息时, 并不是眼球的作用, 当地信徒以餐具名册跳跃行动. 哥斯达黎加朋友翻译了英语最新消息,

featured.title_zh: IMB传教士通过新信徒和当地教会看到神在工作
featured.content: In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo Twenty minutes had passed already. The sun was going down, and they were looking everywhere, but they only saw men in the park. Sophia, an International Mission Board missionary, joined another IMB missionary and Maryam, a South Asian Christian. They went to the park to share the gospel, but approaching a man in their Muslim-majority city was out of the question. They kept walking and watching. Even if they went home without a single conversation, Sophia knew Maryam would want to try again. This woman who had grown up with a distrust of Muslims, now searched a park for a Muslim woman to tell about Jesus. When Sophia first invited her along, Maryam never imagined a Muslim could come to know Jesus. But the more they went out sharing the gospel together, the more God softened her heart. “One day, I found she was sharing in the park by herself, without me,” Sophia said with a laugh. These days, she shares regularly — with classmates, with rickshaw drivers, with women in the park, when she can find them. God transformed Maryam’s heart. He could transform this walk through the park, too. “So we stopped,” Sophia said, “and prayed, ‘God, give us just one woman to talk to.’” Then they spotted her — a girl sitting alone on a bench. Meeting the girl on the bench She looked like other conservative Muslim women in the area, covered in black except for her face. They approached casually, not wanting to frighten her. It was Eid al-Adha – “one of the biggest Muslim holidays here,” Sophia said. They greeted her and asked about her holiday plans. Her name was Tara, and she wasn’t intimidated at all. “You may think I’m a Muslim from the way I dress,” she said, “but actually in my heart, I have left Islam.” “I was a little shocked,” Sophia said, hearing such a bold statement from a stranger. Tara told them she was a university student at a conservative Islamic school, but she had grown disillusioned and discontent with the religion. “ I don’t believe in Islam anymore,” Tara said. Without knowledge of God, she had no one to pray to, and it left her lonely. She’d been searching — Buddhism and Hinduism from friends, even a meeting with atheists, who struck her as unhappy, following only themselves. “Do you know any Christians?” Sophia asked. “Would you like to hear what we believe?” “Sure, please share.” They read about Jesus’ birth, and Tara was hungry for more. When she asked about church, Sophia described their congregation of about 40 believers, many from a Muslim background. Though she wasn’t ready to visit the church, Tara continued her interest in learning. Sophia and Maryam met with her every week in coffee shops, tea shops, Sophia’s home, wherever they could talkthat wasn’t too loud or have “too many ears and eyes” observing them. Finding her closest friend They read through the Gospel of John. One November day in a coffee shop, they reached the passage on the Samaritan woman at the well, and Sophia noticed Tara was crying. “Tara, I see you have tears,” Sophia said. “Let’s stop. Let’s talk about it .” That day, Tara prayed to receive Christ. Soon after, she wanted to visit the church, though nervous how believers would receive her in a hijab. “They will love you,” Sophia told her. “Don’t worry.” Tara went and was welcomed. That Christmas, 80 people packed Sophia’s apartment, singing and dancing in circles. Across the room, Sophia saw Tara, wearing red Christmas garland like a scarf and a smile stretched across her face. “Tara grew up very conservative – music was not even allowed in her home. But now she’s dancing, worshiping the Lord with us with music and songs.” In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo That spring, Tara was baptized.

featured.title_zh: 俄克拉荷马州浸信会加入派遣教会实验室，以加强传教士支持
featured.content: Staff members at First Baptist Church in Wagoner, Oklahoma, evaluate their church’s involvement with missions and missionary support. IMB Photo The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning centered on one question: What does it mean for a church to truly be a sending church? For Mike Wall, a global missions ministry partner of Oklahoma Baptists, the answer begins with churches reclaiming responsibility for the Great Commission. Wall first attended a Sending Church Lab last year in Tulsa with few expectations. He left convinced more churches needed the training. “When I went there, I thought, ‘You’ve got to do this in Oklahoma City,’” Wall said, “because of the content and how much our churches need something just like this.” After observing churches work through the exercises in the lab, Wall said he was encouraged by an emphasis on local church ownership in missions. “We can’t just send our people and say, ‘OK, now this is your job, IMB,’” he said. “We have to do our job in sending, preparing and training the best ‘sent ones’ so that when they get to the field, they can already hit the ground running.” Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement specialist, leads a Sending Church Lab at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City. He is emphasizing the importance of sending churches assessing and equipping future IMB missionaries. IMB Photo Leading the lab was Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement strategist, who developed the concept after seeing the need for stronger relationships between missionaries and local churches. “A Sending Church Lab is our attempt to raise up a host of IMB sending churches,” Wooten said, crediting the North American Mission Board for doing similar events and having successful results. The lab helps churches understand what Wooten calls the church engagement pathway: praying, cooperating, partnering and sending. While many churches faithfully pray, give and go, he said sending requires something more intentional. “Sending includes taking responsibility for an IMB missionary by providing ongoing encouragement, accountability and soul care throughout their term of service,” he explained. During the two-day event, participants gathered around whiteboards to evaluate their church’s missions practices, identify strengths and weaknesses and develop plans for improvement. “We don’t just need to deliver content,” Wooten said. “We need to invite churches to do some work on their own.” Rather than simply listening to presentations, attendees worked through practical questions about prayer, giving, short-term missions, missionary assessment and long-term care. Wooten said churches consistently tell him the greatest benefit is clarity. “They are thankful for clarity on what an IMB sending church is and what our roles and responsibilities are,” he said. For IMB missionaries Peter and Katie Weeks, that clarity is especially valuable. They participated in the lab alongside church leaders. Their real names have been changed to protect their work in Southeast Asia. “There’s no other place I’d rather be during these few days than here,” Peter said. Katie appreciated the interactive nature of the training. “I really appreciate the way they’re actually requiring information from the different churches and encouraging dialogue about how they can go through the steps,” she said. featured.title: A construction engineer in Madagascar became convinced the Bible was true
featured.summary: 🇲🇬Madagascar· 2013
featured.summary_zh: 🇲🇬马达加斯加·2013年
featured.title_zh: 一位在马达加斯加的建筑工程师确信圣经是真的
featured.content: Melias was building things for a living in Madagascar, a construction engineer with a steady trade and, by his own account, no particular expectation that God would interrupt him. In 2013, at twenty-one, God did. It was not dramatic thunder. It was quieter and harder to argue with. "The Holy Spirit convinced my heart that the Bible is true," Melias said. "I found new joy and excitement learning about Jesus through the Scriptures." The book he might have dismissed became the most alive thing in his life. From building houses to building the church He could have kept his new faith as a private comfort and gone on with engineering. Instead he gave it everything. In 2015 he trained for six months as a missionary, and since then he has planted churches and discipled new believers among the Tanala people in Ikongo and the Sakalava in Nosy Be, some of the least reached corners of the island. Now he is training three more Malagasy missionaries to do the same. Madagascar is not a footnote in what God is doing. He is raising up local people like Melias, engineers and tradesmen and ordinary workers, and sending them to their own unreached neighbours. When the Holy Spirit convinces your heart that this is all true, it does not stay a hobby. It becomes the thing you build your life around. He is ready to convince yours.
featured.content_zh:
梅利亚斯在马达加斯加为生计而建东西,他是一位稳定的建筑工程师,据他自己说,他并不特别期望上帝会打断他。 2013年,21时,上帝做到了. 这不是戏剧性的雷声。 更安静,更难争论 "圣灵使我的心相信圣经是真的,"梅利亚斯说.

featured.title: A New Testament sat in his welding workshop until a teenager finally read it
featured.summary: 🇳🇪Agadez· 2000s
featured.summary_zh: 🇳🇪阿加德兹·21世纪初
featured.title_zh: 一本新约圣经一直放在他的焊接车间里，直到一位少年终于读了它。
featured.content: Someone left a New Testament in Pierre's welding workshop in Niger, and for a while it just sat there. He was a teenager, and eventually he picked it up. What he read did not match what he had been told about Christians. It was full of tenderness, of nearness to the poorest, exactly the kind of world his young heart had been quietly hoping was real. Years later he moved to Agadez, out toward the desert, and there he found the thing the book had described. A church family drawn from Benin, Togo, Burkina Faso, France, and Niger, living out what he had only read about. No regret, not for a single day Pierre became a lay missionary, and he does not hedge when he talks about it. "I have never regretted converting to the Christian faith," he says, "not even for a single day." That is a bold thing to say in Niger, where jihadist groups make following Jesus dangerous and his own children have stayed Muslim, something he carries with love and without pressure. Still, no regret. Not one day. He read about a God who is tender toward the poor, and he found that God to be exactly as advertised. Whatever you have heard about Jesus secondhand, He holds up when you finally meet Him yourself. Pierre would tell you to open the book and see.
featured.content_zh:
有人在尼日尔的皮埃尔焊接车间留下了一份新约, 他少年时期,最终他捡到了. 他所读的内容与他被告知的基督徒的情况不符。 它充满了温柔,与最贫穷的人的亲近, 正是他年轻时所希望的世界是真实的。

多年后,他搬到阿加德兹, 向着沙漠, 在那里他发现了书上描述的东西。 一个来自贝宁、多哥、布基纳法索、法国和尼日尔的教会家庭,靠他只读过的东西生活。 没有遗憾,没有一天,皮埃尔成为了一名非专业的传教士,他谈论这件事时不设套.

"我从未后悔过皈依基督教信仰",他说:"即使是一天也没有". 在尼日尔,这是一件大胆的事,在那里,圣战团体追随耶稣,而他自己的孩子则留在穆斯林手中,他带着爱,没有压力。 不过,没有遗憾。 一日不见.

他曾诵读了真主--对于贫民是温和的--他发现真主确是彻知的。 无论你听到什么关于耶稣的二手消息 当你们终于亲眼见到他时 他都挺过来了 Pierre会告诉你打开书看看

featured.title: Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness
featured.source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
featured.summary: Rediscover the wonder of Christmas by focusing on God’s faithfulness and the hope found in Jesus.   The post  Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
featured.summary_zh: 通过关注神的信实和耶稣的盼望，重新发现圣诞节的奇迹。“在圣诞节疲惫中寻找奇迹”一文首次出现在威克里夫。
featured.title_zh: 在圣诞节疲惫中寻找奇迹
featured.content: Christmas is supposed to be a season of wonder. Twinkling lights, familiar songs, meaningful traditions and time with people you love can all point toward the joy of celebrating Jesus’ birth. But when your December calendar fills with responsibilities and expectations, weariness can settle in before you realize it. Maybe you remember a time when Christmas felt different. As a child, you may have counted down the days and experienced joy in even the smallest traditions. As an adult, you might find yourself simply trying to catch your breath as you move from one responsibility to the next. In the middle of trying to make Christmas special for everyone else, it can be easy to miss the wonder yourself. But the Christmas story gives you an opportunity to slow down and remember what this season is really about. In Luke 1, before the story of Jesus’ birth begins, you meet people who knew what it meant to wait, wonder and trust that God was at work even when they couldn’t yet see what He was doing. Weary of Waiting Luke’s account of the life of Jesus doesn’t begin with Jesus’ birth; it begins instead with the story of Zechariah, an elderly priest who was tired of waiting. Zechariah had heard promises of Israel’s rescue from oppression and sin his entire life. That future must have seemed out of reach under Rome’s harsh control. But Zechariah and his wife, Elizabeth, also had an unfulfilled personal longing: “They had no children because Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and they were both very old” ( Luke 1:7, NLT ). One day, as Zechariah performed his duties in the temple, he was chosen to burn incense in the sanctuary — a rare honor with an unexpected result: While Zechariah was in the sanctuary, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the incense altar. Zechariah was shaken and overwhelmed with fear when he saw him. But the angel said, “Don’t be afraid, Zechariah! God has heard your prayer. Your wife, Elizabeth, will give you a son, and you are to name him John. You will have great joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great in the eyes of the Lord. He must never touch wine or other alcoholic drinks. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth. And he will turn many Israelites to the Lord their God. He will be a man with the spirit and power of Elijah. He will prepare the people for the coming of the Lord. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and he will cause those who are rebellious to accept the wisdom of the godly” ( Luke 1:11-17, NLT ). Trusting God in the Waiting An angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah and announced that God had heard his prayer. Elizabeth would have a son named John who would “… prepare the people for the coming of the Lord” ( Luke 1:17b, NLT ). After years of waiting, God answered Zechariah and Elizabeth’s prayer as part of an even bigger story: They would finally have the child they had prayed for, and their son would prepare the way for Jesus. But Zechariah struggled to understand how it could possibly happen: “… ‘How can I be sure this will happen? I’m an old man now, and my wife is also well along in years’” ( Luke 1:18, NLT ). Zechariah could only see what seemed possible based on his circumstances. But God was asking him to trust what He had promised. The angel Gabriel responded by telling Zechariah that he would be unable to speak until the child was born, adding, “For my words will certainly be fulfilled at the proper time” ( Luke 1:20b, NLT ). Maybe you know what it’s like to pray about something for months or even years. It can be hard to keep trusting that God is working when it seems like nothing is changing. Zechariah’s story reminds us that even when we can’t see what God is doing, He is still faithful to His promises. Waiting is woven throughout the Christmas story. Maybe it’s part of your story too. featured.content: IMB Graphic NASHVILLE – As the books closed on the latest fiscal year, receipts for the two Southern Baptist national annual missions offerings underscored the value Southern Baptist churches place on reaching the world with the gospel. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion ministry and other evangelistic efforts to reach North America. IMB President Paul Chitwood said he celebrates what God did in the 2025-26 season and what He is doing now to lead Southern Baptists toward historic generosity. “I thank God for Southern Baptists! With giving through the Lottie Moon offering at an all-time high, churches and individual givers continue to display a heart for the gospel to be proclaimed to every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages,” Chitwood said. The Annie total marked the second highest in NAMB’s history. The record Lottie Moon offering total surpassed last year’s total by more than $5 million and is the best offering in IMB history. “God is giving our generation unprecedented opportunity to send missionaries to the most unreached peoples and places,” Chitwood continued. “Though the challenges faced by our missionaries are enormous, the generosity of Southern Baptists ensures they have what they need to face those challenges and continue in the work while we hold the ropes with our support.” IMB missionary Landon Williams (center) walks with a Chilean pastor and a U.S. pastor on a remote island in Chile. Cooperation and generosity among Southern Baptists fuels the work to reach the uttermost parts of the world with the gospel. IMB Photo National goals for both offerings are set in partnership with Woman’s Missionary Union (WMU) each year. In response to the offering totals, Sandy Wisdom-Martin, executive director-treasurer of WMU, said: “As Southern Baptists, we are all in for His mission. When we give sacrificially, we prioritize the mission of God. Together our fervent prayers, our faithful generosity and our wholehearted obedience become channels for the gospel to reach our neighbors as well as the nations.” For the last 10 years, Southern Baptists have increasingly supported the Annie offering, setting records in seven of the last 10 years. Totals in each of the last four years have surpassed $70 million. “I am so grateful to the pastors and churches for the faithfulness and generosity they have demonstrated through this offering,” said NAMB president Kevin Ezell. “As I travel and speak in churches of all sizes, I love seeing the posters in the hallways showing their offering goals. For some it is a few hundred dollars, for others several thousand.” The Annie Armstrong offering supports more than 3,000 missionaries in North America, including the ongoing work of church planting in the U.S. and Canada. In 2025, Southern Baptists planted the largest number of churches, 699, since 2016. Including church plants and replants, Southern Baptists have surpassed 700 new churches in four of the last five years. More than 12,000 churches have been planted since 2010. To go along with the increased giving totals to the SBC’s missions offerings, Southern Baptists have also increased their local outreach efforts, indicating that the focus is not just on giving but on sending. Baptism totals have increased in each of the last five years, recovering from the pandemic-year low in 2020 to surpass the 2017 total. The five consecutive years of increase marked the first such streak in approximately 75 years. To Jordan Adams, unheard of things like 38 baptisms in one worship service have become “heard of” for his congregation. featured.summary: Ken and Sally discovered a way to give God’s Word — a gift they’d had access to their whole lives — to others.    The post  Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
featured.summary_zh: Ken和Sally发现了一种方法，可以将上帝的话语--这是他们一生都能接触到的礼物--传递给他人。“活出管理和信仰的遗产”一文首次出现在威克里夫。
featured.title_zh: 活出管理和信仰的遗产
featured.content: What did your journey to faith look like? Perhaps it was a story of how God showed up in the midst of uncertainty, doubt or fears. Maybe it involved Him seeking you out and rescuing you. Or maybe you grew up in a Christian household and your story is a bit different — perhaps your family regularly read the Bible together and have always known about Jesus’ love. Ken Trager was raised that way. He reflected, “I think when you’re raised in a Christian home … and you have the routines of a life that is built around church and prayer, you just take it for granted.” He added, “It was just the air I breathed.” For Ken and his wife, Sally, faith was always part of their stories. They were each raised in Christian homes, followed Christ, got baptized and had parents who faithfully modeled church attendance, prayer and generosity.  Ken and Sally’s paths eventually crossed at Greenville University in southern Illinois, where they met and fell in love. They went on to build a life centered around family, faith and service. Ken spent his career as a teacher and coach while Sally worked as an accountant, and together they raised two children. Now retired, they’ve moved to be closer to their children and grandchildren, giving them a new opportunity to pour into the next generation. Through all those years and seasons, the faith Ken and Sally had seen modeled by their families continued to shape their home. Early in their marriage, Ken and Sally met a mentor who encouraged the couple to go deeper with their faith — to study Scripture, ask questions and wrestle honestly with what they believed. It was an important season of discovering that the faith that had been passed down from their families could also become something they personally owned and lived out together. What Do You Take for Granted? Years later, the couple experienced an aha moment when they were introduced to Wycliffe at an event. There, Ken and Sally heard story after story from people who had received Scripture in their own languages. Something clicked for Sally: “We’ve never known a day where we couldn’t access the Bible. And these people have just longed for it, and they’re finally getting it.” For the first time, something that had always surrounded the couple became visible — and it was a gift they could no longer take for granted . Ken and Sally had spent years thinking about the importance of God’s Word. Seeing people receive Scripture in their own languages helped them understand just how extraordinary that access is. “The power of salvation comes through that,” Ken said. “I can’t think of … [a more] important work than providing God’s Word to everybody in the world.” Sally agreed. “To have His Word is as if we’re hearing the voice of God,” she said. “God works through His Word.” This conviction — for people around the world to be able to access Scripture for themselves — became one of the reasons Ken and Sally prioritized a place in their giving for Wycliffe. But it also became part of a larger question about generosity they had been asking themselves for years: “If everything we have is a gift from God, what does it look like to live generously with it?” A Generous Heart Generosity, like faith, was something Ken and Sally had grown up around. Ken remembers his dad giving him money to put in the offering plate, and Sally remembers watching her parents give not just to their church but to people and organizations in need. Sally’s father especially enjoyed giving anonymously. As Ken and Sally have grown older, they’ve learned that generosity isn’t simply about giving a certain percentage or checking a box; it’s about continually asking what it means to have a generous heart . For Ken, the question of what it means to be generous has become what he calls “Kingdom Advancement Giving.” When contemplating giving, he asks, “Is this going to advance the Kingdom for God’s glory?” That question has shaped the way the couple thinks about which individuals and organizations they

你的信仰之旅是什么样子的? 也许这是上帝如何在不确定、怀疑或恐惧中出现的故事。 也许这涉及到他寻找你 并救你。 或者你在一个基督教家庭长大,你的故事有点不同——也许你的家人经常一起阅读圣经,并且一直知道耶稣的爱。 肯崔格是那样长大的

他回想道 , “ 我想当你在基督教家庭长大... 你有一个在教堂和祷告周围建造的日常生活, 你只是把它视为理所当然。 ” 他又说:“只是我呼吸的空气。” 对于肯和他的妻子莎莉来说,信仰总是他们的故事的一部分.

他们各自在基督教家中长大,跟随基督,接受洗礼,并有忠实的模范教会出席,祈祷和慷慨的父母. 肯和莎莉的道路最终在伊利诺伊州南部的格林维尔大学交叉,在那里他们相遇并坠入爱河. 他们继续建立一个以家庭、信仰和服务为中心的生活。

肯在萨利担任会计期间度过了教师和教练的生涯,两人一起抚养两个孩子. 他们已经退休了, 他们已经搬到更亲近他们的儿孙, 给他们一个新的机会, 注入下一代。 在那些年和季节中,肯和莎莉所见到的由家人塑造的信仰继续塑造自己的家园.

早年的婚姻中,肯和莎莉结识了一位导师,他鼓励这对夫妇更深入地信仰——学习圣经,提出问题,并诚实地与所相信的东西搏斗. 这是一个重要的季节,发现从家人传下来的信仰也可能成为他们个人拥有和共同生活的东西. 你拿什么给格兰特?

多年后,夫妇俩在一次活动上被介绍到怀克利夫(Wycliffe)时,经历了一段愉快的时刻. 在那里,肯和莎莉从以自己语言接受圣经的人那里听到一个接一个的故事. “我们从未知道有一天我们无法阅读圣经。

而这些人也只是渴望, 第一次,一直包围着这对夫妇的东西变得明显——这是他们不能再视为理所当然的礼物了. 肯和莎莉花了多年时间思考上帝之言的重要性.

看到人们用自己的语言接受圣经 有助于他们理解这种访问是多么非凡 肯说,“救赎的力量来自此”。 " 我无法想象......比向全世界每个人提供上帝的话更重要的工作。 " 萨莉同意了 ”她说,

“真主通过他的话而工作。” 这种信念——让世界各地的人们能够为自己获得圣经——成为肯和莎莉在为威克利夫奉献一个位置时优先考虑的原因之一.

但是,它也成为了一个更大的问题的一部分,即他们多年来一直问自己:“如果我们所拥有的一切是上帝的礼物,那么与它慷慨相处是什么样子?” 和信仰一样 善良的心是肯和莎莉成长的

肯记得父亲给了他钱放进祭品盘中,莎莉记得看着她的父母不仅把钱送给他们的教堂,还送给需要帮助的人和组织. Sally的父亲特别喜欢匿名赠送。 肯和莎莉已经长大了, 他们已经了解到慷慨不只是给予一定的百分比或检查一个盒子。

需要不断问, 对肯来说,慷慨意味着什么的问题已经变成了他所谓的“提高国王地位”的问题。 当他考虑施舍的时候,他问道:"这难道是为了真主的荣耀而推动王国吗? 这个问题决定了夫妻双方对哪些个人和组织的看法

featured.title_zh: IMB寻求教师、医护人员、商业专业人士担任传教士
featured.content: IMB missionary Dr. Heidi Haun, left, checks on patients at Baptist Medical Centre in Nalerigu, Ghana. There are needed roles for IMB missionaries in healthcare, ministering to the needs of local populations and utilizing this time to minister to spiritual needs. IMB Photo When most Southern Baptists think of missionaries, they often picture church planters and evangelists. But leaders with the International Mission Board say some of the greatest needs today are for professionals whose work happens behind the scenes. IMB leaders report that critical roles such as teachers, healthcare workers, counselors, accountants, logistics specialists and member care personnel are helping advance the Great Commission in ways many churches never see. Doreen Baker, IMB director of TCK (third culture kid or missionary kid) education, sees a constant need for education professionals. Teachers are needed in international schools, which cover a variety of global educational entities, and in other settings to provide for missionary kids and their educational needs. “Teachers are significant in that not only are they providing instruction for students, but they are an integral part of the core missionary task ,” Baker said. “We also have great needs for consultants to support our families on the field with their children’s education in many ways.” Baker previously served 25 years teaching in Asia and experienced how education creates access to missions where traditional pathways may be limited. IMB missionary Ellie Bohrer teaches a 12th grade World Views class at Black Forest Academy in Germany. The IMB is seeking other educators, like Bohrer, who are willing to use their skills on the mission field. IMB Photo Scott Ray, IMB senior director of global deployment, noted that many missionary positions go unfilled simply because they fall outside traditional perceptions of missionary service. He said professional skills can provide both practical ministry support and access to countries where traditional missionary visas are difficult to obtain. Opportunities exist for finance professionals, veterinarians, medical workers, Send Relief personnel and others. Healthcare remains one of the most strategic areas in demand. Tom Hicks, IMB director of global health strategies, said many medical professionals have the wrong perception about mission work. “We do have an issue where people will select out because they don’t think that what they do is useful on the mission field,” he said. In reality, Hicks said many areas across the globe are increasingly seeking family medicine physicians, internists, pediatricians, pediatric nurse practitioners, OB providers, physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech pathologists and lactation consultants. The need is especially significant in sub-Saharan Africa, where young populations create a growing demand for pediatric care. Healthcare professionals also provide a unique advantage in countries that restrict missionary activity. “Missionaries with a vocational value, like healthcare missionaries, have opportunities to go places that others can’t go,” Hicks said. Another often-overlooked ministry is member care, which focuses on the spiritual, emotional, mental and relational health of IMB missionaries. Chris Martin is the IMB director of global member care. “Member care missionaries stand alongside those missionaries that are thought of traditionally as church planters or evangelists and support them,” Martin said. Many who serve in these roles come from counseling backgrounds and help missionaries navigate stress, conflict, grief and other challenges that can affect long-term ministry effectiveness. Martin compares their role to Aaron and Hur in Exodus 19, holding up Moses’ arms during battle, strengthening those serving on the front lines. IMB missionary Glen Garner uses his business skills and experience as the logistics director for missionaries serving globally. He lives in Lima, Peru, with his wife, Shannon

featured.title_zh: 全球传教士合作伙伴通过IMB团队扩展福音工作
featured.content: Rebeca Couto, a global missionary partner from the Azores islands, practices writing characters with her tutor in Japan. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto poses with her violin. Couto is a professional violinist who is serving as a global missionary partner with the IMB in Japan. Doors have opened for her to use her skills with evangel ical Japanese musicians who perform. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto moved from one volcanic archipelago to another, leaving Portugal’s Azores islands to anchor her life in Japan. The percentage of evangelical Christians in the Azores and Japan is similar, with both populations under 1%. Couto is a fourth-generation Christian, a rarity on the small islands. She is one of few, if any, believers in the Azores with such a long spiritual lineage. This rich legacy shaped her and prepared her for ministry. “I’ve always understood the Great Commission as a call for all believers and all disciples of Christ to be missionaries, wherever they are, whatever they’re doing, and whatever God has equipped them with,” Couto said. Couto’s great-grandfather became a Christian through the witness of missionaries from the United Kingdom. Later, missionaries from the Foreign Mission Board, now the International Mission Board, started the first Baptist work in the Azores by planting an English-speaking church near an American military base. A Baptist Brazilian couple planted a Portuguese-speaking church, which became the congregation where Couto grew up and was commissioned as a missionary. Ministry has been passed down through the generations of her family. Couto’s father has pastored for 20 years, and both of her parents have been involved in ministry for most of their lives. Couto now serves in Japan as a global missionary partner, a missionary who is financially supported by a sending church or organization in their home country and serves with IMB teams. Close to 400 GMPs currently serve on IMB teams around the world. Language learning Couto is immersed in language study in Yokohama, Japan. She had a head start before she even arrived. After graduating from high school, Couto moved from the Azores to Lisbon to pursue a degree in music. She spent hours on public transportation and wanted a challenge to pass the time. She decided to study Japanese because she thought it sounded beautiful. At the time, she had no intention of becoming a missionary in the traditional sense. However, the more she learned about the language and the culture, her burden for the lost grew. She began researching Christianity in Japan. “I understood how bleak the scenario was, and how much the country needed Jesus. I struggled with that calling because the doors were closed, and it didn’t seem possible to come to Japan for a myriad of reasons,” Couto said. After finishing master’s degrees in music and violin performance, along with a seminary degree, Couto was considering pursuing a Ph.D. or returning to seminary when her seminary professors, IMB missionaries Jonathan and Bethany Sharp, contacted her about serving as a missionary in Japan. They introduced her to the GMP program and invited her to attend a missions immersion school they piloted . Music to their ears As a professional violinist, Couto brought her violin to Japan, unsure of what opportunities existed, but she knew her call to the mission field somehow involved her gifting. “I see myself as having been called to serve through music. I never even conceived doing missions while excluding the violin entirely,” Couto said.
